candidates.statement: Pharmacies located within a hospital, or standalone pharmacies that are part of a health system, 17 frequently provide compounded drug products for administration within the hospital or health 18 system. 2 Some of these compounders seek to compound drugs under section 503A of the 19 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 353a) and others have registered 20 with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA, the Agency, or we) as outsourcing facilities and 21 are subject to section 503B of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 353b). 3

Second, it addresses the provision concerning compounded drug products that are 29 essentially copies of a commercially available drug product (section 503A(b)(1)(D) of the FD&C 30 Act). candidates.statement: Although compounded drug products can serve an important need, they pose a higher risk to 111 patients than FDA-approved drug products. Compounded drug products are not FDA-approved, 112 which means they have not undergone FDA premarket review for safety, effectiveness, and 113 quality. For these reasons, compounded drug products should only be used when an FDA- 114 approved product is not available to meet the medical needs of an individual patient. 115
candidates.context: Compounded drug products can serve an important role for patients in hospitals and health 104 systems whose medical needs cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug product, such as a patient 105 who has an allergy and needs a medication to be made without a certain dye, or an elderly patient 106 or a child who cannot swallow a pill and needs a medicine in a liquid form that is not otherwise 107 available. Many hospital and health system pharmacies, for example, routinely compound oral 108 liquids from tablets or other dosage forms for use in pediatric units. 12 7 See section 503A(a)(2) of the FD&C Act.

candidates.statement: Since the 2012 fungal meningitis outbreak, FDA has investigated numerous other outbreaks and 132 other serious adverse events, including deaths, associated with compounded drug products that 133 were contaminated or otherwise unsafe. For example, in 2019, FDA received a report 134 concerning seven patients who received an injectable drug product compounded with L- 135 glutathione and experienced adverse events consistent with reactions patients experience with 136 high levels of endotoxins. FDA’s testing of the L-glutathione samples confirmed higher levels 137 of endotoxin than is appropriate based on the dose of L-glutathione received intravenously. The 138 L-glutathione powder the compounding pharmacies received was labeled with “Caution: Dietary 139 Supplement” and should not have been used to compound sterile injectable drug products. 14 In 140 2017, FDA received adverse event reports concerning at least 43 patients who were administered 141 eye injections of a compounded drug product during cataract surgery and later experienced 142 various adverse events, including vision impairment. FDA’s investigation revealed the presence 143 of an excipient in an amount that was much greater than what is found in FDA-approved 144 ophthalmic products. 15
candidates.context: In 2012, contaminated injectable drug products that a compounding pharmacy shipped to 127 patients and healthcare practitioners across the country caused a fungal meningitis outbreak that 128 resulted in over 60 deaths and over 750 cases of infection. 13 This was the most serious of a long 129 history of outbreaks associated with contaminated compounded drug products. 130 FDA has also identified many pharmacies that compounded drug products under insanitary 147 conditions whereby the drug products may have been contaminated with filth or rendered 148 injurious to health and that shipped the compounded drug products made under these conditions 149 to patients and health care providers in large volumes across the country. 16 The longer a 150 compounded drug product that is contaminated is held by a pharmacist or physician before 151

candidates.statement: To the extent that hospitals and health systems have a need for compounded drug products, FDA 157 encourages them to obtain such products from outsourcing facilities. Compounders 158 that elect to become outsourcing facilities must register with FDA, are subject to CGMP 159 requirements, and are inspected by FDA according to a risk-based schedule (section 503B of the 160 FD&C Act). This helps to mitigate the risk that their drug products will be contaminated or 161 otherwise made under substandard conditions. 162
candidates.context: C. Compounding by Hospitals and Health Systems 155 However, we are aware that hospitals and health systems have a variety of distribution practices 164 for drug products that have been compounded in their pharmacies. For example, some 165 pharmacies compound drug products only for use in the hospital in which the pharmacy is 166 located (e.g., for the treatment of patients during a hospital admission, or for use in the hospital’s 167 emergency room), while some health system pharmacies distribute their drug products to other 168 facilities within their health system (e.g., to other hospitals, clinics, infusion centers, or long-term 169 care facilities within the health system). 170

In considering action to achieve hospital and health 217 system compliance with the prescription requirement in section 503A of the FD&C Act, FDA 218 intends to focus on practices that pose the greatest risks to public health. candidates.statement: As stated above, to qualify for the exemptions under section 503A of the FD&C Act from 243 sections 501(a)(2)(B), 502(f)(1), and 505(a), a drug product must be compounded by a licensed 244 pharmacist or licensed physician who does not compound regularly or in inordinate amounts any 245 drug product that is essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product. 18 Pursuant to 246 section 503A(b)(2) of the FD&C Act, a compounded drug product is not essentially a copy of a 247 commercially available drug product if a change is made to the commercially available drug 248 product for an identified individual patient, and the prescribing practitioner has determined that 249 the change will produce a significant difference for that patient. As described in FDA’s 503A 250 copies guidance, if a compounder intends to rely on such a determination to establish that a 251 compounded drug is not essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product, the 252 compounder should ensure that the determination is documented on the prescription. A drug 253 product is not considered to be commercially available if the drug product has been discontinued 254 and is no longer marketed or the drug product appears on the FDA drug shortage list in effect 255 under section 506E of the FD&C Act. 256
candidates.context: 2. Compounding of Drug Products That Are Essentially Copies 241 The restrictions on compounding drug products that are essentially copies of commercially 258 available drug products help to ensure that pharmacies, Federal facilities, and physicians do not 259 compound drug products under section 503A of the FD&C Act for use in patients who could use 260 an approved product. Compounding drug products that are essentially copies of these products 261 unnecessarily exposes patients to drug products that have not been shown to be safe and 262 effective. In addition to the immediate public health risks, the limitation in section 503A of the 263 FD&C Act on producing drug products that are essentially copies of a commercially available 264 drug product protects the integrity of the new drug and abbreviated new drug approval processes. 265 Applicants would be less likely to invest in, and seek

Additionally, decisions about when and how to use medications are 281 often made under medication-use policies set by a pharmacy and therapeutics (P&T) committee 282 (or its equivalent) that prescribers are expected to follow. 19 The P&T committees are comprised 283 of medical staff that develop policies to support the appropriate use of medications within the 284 hospital and health system. Such P&T committees are common in hospitals and health systems 285 and the activities they perform are a requirement for accreditation by some accrediting 286 organizations, such as The Joint Commission. 20 For example, a P&T committee may determine 287 that all patients in a neonatal unit administered certain oral medications should receive a 288 compounded liquid dosage form because the approved drug product, available only in a tablet 289 formulation, is medically inappropriate for them. 290

candidates.statement: 23 Such a limit mitigates concerns about the amount and scope of distribution of the compounded drug product. FDA selected 24 hours as the window within which compounded drug products be used or discarded because the Agency has heard from stakeholders that non-patient-specific drugs are needed for emergency uses. FDA anticipates that non-patient-specific compounded drugs that are kept on hand for longer periods can and should be obtained from outsourcing facilities because outsourcing facilities can compound and distribute drugs without receiving patient- specific prescriptions and, because they are subject to CGMPs, conduct appropriate stability tests and have more robust sterility assurance practices.
candidates.context: However, administration within the hospital or health system includes scenarios where administration of a drug product is initiated at the hospital or health system facility, where the drug product is later transferred with the patient when he or she leaves the facility. For example, an infusion may be initiated in the health care facility and subsequently transitioned to the home setting using the same IV bag containing the product that was compounded by the health care facility. 24 For more examples of insanitary conditions, see FDA’s guidance for industry Insanitary Conditions at Compounding Facilities (November 2020).
